content: The hop plant, belonging to the genus Humulus, is a small group of flowering plants native to the temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. The female flowers, commonly referred to as hops, are utilized as flavoring agents and stabilizers in the brewing of beer. Hops are part of the Cannabaceae family, which also includes the genus Cannabis (commonly known as hemp). While often called a hop vine, it is technically a bine, as it climbs using stout stems with stiff hairs rather than tendrils or other appendages. Hops are perennial herbaceous plants that produce new shoots in early spring and die back to their cold-hardy rhizomes in autumn. The shoots grow rapidly, with peak growth rates reaching 20–50 cm per week (approximately 1–3 inches per day). Depending on the available support structures, hop bines can grow to heights of 5 to 15 meters (16 to 50 feet). The leaves are opposite, with petioles measuring 7–12 cm (2.75–4.75 inches) and cordate-based, palmately lobed blades that are 12–25 cm (4.75–10 inches) long and broad. The leaf edges are coarsely toothed. When the bines run out of climbing material, horizontal shoots emerge between the leaves of the main stem, forming a network of intertwined stems. Species There are three main species of hops, with one species having five distinct varieties: Humulus japonicus (syn. H. scandens), or Asian hop, has leaves with 5–7 lobes and is native to Eastern Asia. Humulus lupulus, or common hop, has leaves with 3–5 lobes and is found in Europe, Western Asia, and North America. Its varieties include: H. lupulus var. lupulus (Europe, Western Asia) H. lupulus var. cordifolius (Eastern Asia) H. lupulus var. lupuloides (syn. H. americanus) (Eastern North America) H. lupulus var. neomexicanus (Western North America) H. lupulus var. pubescens (Midwest North America) Humulus yunnanensis, or Yunnan hop, has leaves with 3–5 lobes that are densely hairy on the underside and is endemic to Southeast Asia, particularly Yunnan, China. Brewers' hops are specific cultivars propagated through asexual reproduction. Cultivation and History The first recorded instance of hop cultivation dates back to 736 CE in the Hallertau region of present-day Germany, which remains a major production center, accounting for approximately 25% of global hop production. The use of hops in brewing was first mentioned in 1067 by Abbess Hildegard of Bingen. Hops were introduced to British beers in the early 1500s, and hop cultivation began in the United States in 1629. Today, major hop production centers include Germany, the United States (notably Washington State), Belgium, the Czech Republic, and the UK (Kent and Worcestershire). Other significant regions include Xinjiang (China), Tasmania (Australia), Lublin (Poland), and Chuvashia (Russia). New Zealand is a leading producer of organic hops. Before mechanization in the late 1960s, hop harvesting required large amounts of labor, creating significant social impacts. In Kent, England, families from London's East End would migrate annually to work in the hop fields, living in hoppers' huts during September. This tradition became part of British cultural history. Romany travelers also played a significant role in hop harvesting. Propagation and Pests European hops are propagated through nursery plants or cuttings, which are planted in hills filled with fine leaf mold. The density of planting varies, with 3–5 holes per square meter. Hop cultivation is profitable but risky due to susceptibility to pests. Significant insect pests include the European corn borer (Ostrinia nubilalis) and the hop froghopper (Aphrophora interrupta). Aphids (Myzus humuli) can damage hops in June and July, particularly if the plants are already weakened by root damage caused by the larvae of the otter moth (Phalaena humuli). Other pests include the larvae of the common swift, ghost moth, and orange swift, as well as various Lepidoptera species that feed on foliage. Harvesting By the end of the first year, poles are placed in the hills to support the bines. In the second year, full-sized poles (5–6 meters long) are set, with two poles per hill. The bines are loosely fastened to the poles. In the Northern Hemisphere, hops begin flowering in late June or early July. The female plants produce scaly seed vessels, which are hand-picked when the seeds form around late August. The harvested hops are dried, aired for a few days, and packed into sacks for market distribution. Uses Beer Hops contain two primary acids: alpha acids and beta acids. Alpha acids have mild antibiotic and bacteriostatic effects against Gram-positive bacteria, favoring the activity of brewing yeast during fermentation. Hops impart bitterness, flavor, and aroma to beer, depending on when they are added during the brewing process. Bittering hops are boiled with the beer to produce bitterness, while hops added later contribute flavor and aroma. Dry hopping, the addition of hops after boiling, enhances aroma with minimal bitterness. The bitterness of hops is measured in International Bitterness Units (IBUs). Beta acids do not isomerize during boiling and have minimal impact on beer flavor. However, they contribute to aroma and can oxidize to form sulfur compounds, such as dimethyl sulfide (DMS), which can produce off-flavors. Noble hops, low in bitterness and high in aroma, are traditional European cultivars used in pale lagers. English ales use varieties like Fuggle and Golding, while North American varieties include Cascade and Willamette. Highly hopped styles, such as India Pale Ale (IPA), are known for their pronounced bitterness and complex flavors. Medicinal Use Hops have well-documented medicinal properties. Two active compounds, humulene and lupuline, are of particular interest. Dried female buds contain methylbutenol, which has a mild sedative effect on the central nervous system and is used to treat insomnia, stress, and anxiety. Hop tea or beer can aid sleep. Hops also stimulate gastric juice production and have antibacterial, antiviral, and antimycobacterial properties. They contain flavonoids and estrogen precursors, which are under investigation for potential health benefits. Fiber The hop stem is tough and flexible, with a tenacious fiber that has been used to make cloth and paper. Hops are closely related to hemp, another fiber-producing plant. Other Uses Hops are an ingredient in Julmust, a Swedish carbonated beverage popular in December. Tender young hop shoots, available for a brief period in spring, were historically consumed by the poor as a substitute for asparagus. They are now considered a delicacy in parts of Germany, Belgium, and England, served raw, boiled, or fried. In Veneto, Italy, they are used in risotto or frittata. Wild hops are also consumed by livestock. Mature hop bines are sometimes used as decorations in public houses or kitchens, with a traditional belief that they bring good luck. In some regions, hop bines are sold for decorative purposes, providing an alternative income for hop farmers. Hops have also been used to increase breast milk production in women with low supply.
